utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of the transcript on Monday, you were asked about your alleged ties with the SDS. You denied having been an SDS man. Is that still your position?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it is. First of all, I was not a member of the SDS, and there were no ties between us with regard to any military activities. Within my structure, I had my superior command which was, in my view, the only responsible factor that I had to establish any ties with in implementing their orders. It was the Main Staff of the VRS, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you tell them that? Did you tell them that you were not a party man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I tried to make it known to them so that they wouldn't harbour any such feelings or interpretations. I didn't want them to try to achieve such an atmosphere. I knew full well that they couldn't count on me in that regard. I think they simply wanted to count on some people from the Main Staff to try and portray the existence of some party ties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to show you some entries from the Mladic diaries.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P1473. In the Serbian can we have page 267, and in English 264.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall a meeting of the 7th of August -- what year is that? Probably 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where is Ostrelj?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think I've mentioned already that Ostrelj is an area or a topographic feature which is close to Drvar. That's all I know. It is somewhere in the territory of Republika Srpska in the so-called Banja Luka Krajina or the Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page. Is it stated here that you told him that you were no party man? Let me find that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please. In the English too. The next page in both versions. This is fine in the English. It is in the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian, look at the last paragraph and what you said?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Having arrived --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No, the last item, "I have the feeling."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "I have a feeling that there is a belief in the General Staff that I am Karadzic's man and that I am an SDS man. No one --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "No one knows."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "No one knows how --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Hurt I have been by this."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, "Hurt I have been by this."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's not only that you told them that you were not a party man, you also told them that you were hurt by such interpretations.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at 65 ter 9139, which is a letter you were shown by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please zoom in for the General, the top of the page -- sorry, the bottom of the page. I'm interested in the underlined sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of what this is about. The underlined part: "The people from the inner circle of the General Staff of the VRS warned me that there is a general view of myself being an SDS general, a general of the Assembly or a Chetnik general, Karadzic's man, a party man, and such like."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You may stop there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these adjectives were ascribed to me. I'm not really clear as to why they needed it. First of all, there was no basis for it. I do know, however, that perhaps word had reached the General Staff that the SRK forces stood their ground and undertook appropriate measures to protect their area, perhaps creating the impression of the corps being praised, perhaps unduly, and they must have created an opinion in the sense that my successes should be belittled to show that perhaps I was pretentious and so on and so forth. I simply know that I had to take a lot of it in a situation which required activities of different kind, not discussing such topics. One had to bear it all in order to emerge honourably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You deny that in the last paragraph. General, would it have been something bad that you were an Assembly general or the president's general? Whose generals were the other ones, those who held it against you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us be clear on it. I would tell them -- well, allegedly my promotion, or so they believed, was proposed by President Karadzic, and I asked him, "Well, who signed your promotional decrees?" It was understood what I meant, but still there was the impression that a decree was signed on my behalf as if it were something special. That was one thing. Another thing, I don't see why there should be any negative consequences stemming from it. If the person has achieved what was required of him -- of him and of his units in -- in combat engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the last paragraph on page 1, and then we'll go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. "I was none of that. I was a simple Serb, a professional soldier who has dedicated his entire life to the army, thus confirming that I only want to do my job conscientiously." I think that's clear, and I think it was clear to them too.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 3, please. I'm interested in a paragraph there. The one in the middle, just above the underlined part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "It was my great --"

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "It was my great wish with your approval to leave the VRS honourably and decently, and I am proud of it. I was preoccupied with my job in the army, not with the SDS, but I see now that I may not be allowed to leave honourably."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would this position persist if another party had been in power? Well, this calls for speculation. I will withdraw it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it is relevant or not, but since this letter was raised by both parties, General, can I ask you what it was that you said you couldn't carry out? The part of the order you couldn't carry out. Could you tell us in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. It requires a few sentences so as to make it clear. During that period, there was an assessment and a decision that was made that the SRK as a military structure would practically cease to exist. Because of the restructuring of the entire VRS, the SRK basically -- or its units and its personnel fell under the Hercegovina Corps commanded by General Grubac. There was a hand-over in the units, and there were difficulties with the procedure during some post-war events. There were a lot of inoperative or damaged pieces and so on and so forth. However, we still had to go through the process of hand-over. In a string of attempts - at least that's the way I saw it - there was an intent on his part to undermine my value and the worth of the units I had commanded. He issued an order that I should personally count every single rifle, as if giving me a job, something to do, because I was out of work apparently. And he wanted to make an inventory list and hand it over personally to General Grubac. I hope that people would understand that it was not my job to do. As the corps commander, no one could order me or put me in a position to be in the role of a company officer, because it was the job of such company officers to keep records of company weapons and assets. It could only take place in junior units. I had to resist such an attempt, because I didn't want to see myself reduced to such levels while I had exercised my duty properly. I had to confirm that I refused to do it. It fell in the category of directly opposing an order. I did not hesitate to do it. I said, "There you go. There is a Military Court. Deal with it through the Military Court." If a person in charge of such proceedings wanted to have them instituted, then such a person would need to decide whether it was within my remit to do it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. We will receive it as the next -- as the next Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2901, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, on Monday, on page 9 of the transcript, you were asked -- it was put forward to you that you did not know of any cases of my orders not being observed or honoured. You answered that you never had occasion to be alone with the two of us, one on one, or with both of us. My question is whether my order of transforming the general headquarters to the Main Staff was put into practice.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff remained as such. It retained its name, the Main Staff of the VRS, of course. It maintained its name. It wasn't transformed into a General Staff. So this order did not take effect as far as I can recall, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was my order about the position of General Mladic, was it also honoured?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, D2155. 2155. Were you aware before that of tensions between military and civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware. What could be felt was a climate, an atmosphere of -- which I could label without being tied fast to that characterization. There is a saying, "One people, two masters," which meant -- well, I did feel a certain degree of ignoring of the existence of civilian structures among the people we are discussing. First and foremost, among those -- some of those in the Main Staff. I know that they raised issues, saying that there were activities being carried out that bore the hallmarks of smuggling, black market operations concerning assets and resources, and that there -- there was the Main Staff who wanted to stop such practices, that it was detrimental to the army, and such tensions intensified until a conflict broke out between the two of you. As far as my explanation went, I did say that I was never there in your company where I could see what were your resentments and who is not observing whose direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. On pages 10 and 11 of Monday's transcript, you were questioned, and you were shown quotations from RS Assembly session mid-April 1995. I would like to ask you if you were there, if you were at the Main Staff, did you receive my letter which was sent two weeks after that Assembly session at Sanski Most? Sent to corps commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that has a very tenuous link to the topics raised in cross-examination, because the cross-examination was solely about what was said during the Assembly session in April of 1995 and involved putting quotes to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I explore the nature of the conflict or rift between the two persons. I would allow the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this letter forwarded to you, that letter which I sent to all corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like nothing more than to confirm firmly whether it was forwarded to me or not. I'm trying to recall the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we take a look at page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't have to read it out loud, but could you please read for yourself the second box starting with "Possible coup d'etat," "Military coup." Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this fit with your knowledge about the tensions between the military and the civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is exactly what I wanted to say. What follows from this, and I confirm that without reading this paragraph, is that that tension between those actors had been felt before, had long been felt, and now one can conclude that after a long period of tension it had to come to a head in terms of refusal to obey orders issued by the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to show you a letter, 1D2002, dated 20th April 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we do not have any translation. You could look for yourself. For the benefit of the Chamber and all others, let me explain this. This is an official note by Momcilo Mandic about his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, that is not the way in the case of untranslated documents. You are not giving evidence. You need to put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, for the benefit of everybody else in the courtroom, then my question is: Can you tell us what this official note is about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see this official note, and of course I see what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's not a proper question in redirect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure if it is an official note. Do you follow, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we can take a look at this document. It has its own number, and this person in his capacity as advisor to the president notified a person who no longer was a minister, and this was an official note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. You are not giving evidence. We do not know what this document is about. You need to put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the General what this official note was, what it spoke about, what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm overlapping. That's exactly a leading question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the General this:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain this document to the Chamber, its nature and its content?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. It is sufficient to read it. It implies a certain amount of pressure being exerted on certain structures without apparent reason. However, what I can say now is not written here, and it was not discussed, but I do know that some -- I received information. This is how I know. I don't know when exactly or where. I know that some people from the political leadership and from the government would be detained at the Main Staff. They would be intercepted on a road and then detained at the Main Staff for a number of days. I think that this occurred -- I mean -- I mean, I think that this concerned the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you read out loud the last sentence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, with respect, no. Dr. Karadzic has to find out -- has to demonstrate some link between the witness and the document. The witness has effectively said he knows nothing about the document, and Dr. Karadzic persists to try and have the document read out in court. It's not proper questions in redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, before saying what you knew with respect to this document, could you tell us first what this document is about, who wrote this document, and what it is? First could you read out the -- the logo, the letters that -- that are behind the logo. Probably "Republika Srpska." Could you read out those lines.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood. It says in the letterhead below the emblem, "Republika Srpska, Office of the President of the Republic, Sarajevo." After that, on the left-hand side, date, 20th of April, 1995. Number official SL, meaning official, 1/95. Subject, official note. And then the text and the contents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the signatory? Who wrote this letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was signed presumably by the person who wrote it, and it says here "Advisor to the president," I presume president of the republic, "Momcilo Mandic, MA."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why was Mandic using the letterhead of the office of the president?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell. I see from the contents that he encountered a problem and he wanted to notify the president of that. What authority he had in terms of using the official memos, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And before you put a question, you need to lay some foundation why you are going to put this document to the witness, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the General said that he was aware of intentions and misunderstandings between the civilian and military structures, and he labelled it as a situation of one people, two lead -- masters. He did not know of this document, but he heard about civilian authority representatives being detained and arrested. This letterhead is not of the president but of the office of the president, and this person used to be advisor to the president. I wanted to ask the General whether this document, and to what extent, reflected what he knew about conflicts between the military and the civilian structures. And the last sentence of that note is very important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think you could ask the question independent of this document, Mr. Karadzic. Why don't you do that now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, did you know -- General, in those tensions which -- which side did they favour, certain structures within the military leadership? Loyalty to which side, they declared their loyalty to which side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me give you this answer and of course to the Chamber. It is certain, as far as I know, concerning your question who favoured and who aligned themselves to which side. This did not have any particular influence on the structure of the SRK, its forces, its structures. The corps was so busy with combat activities and fighting again the forces that I referred to many times so far, that we could not follow developments or ruptures that would be detrimental to us among those at the top. Those conflicts could not influence us or prevent us in carrying out our defensive duties along the front line. This is the first thing I can tell you, and I stand 100 per cent by that assertion. Furthermore, I'm not asserting this, but I can tell you that I had a feeling that there were people aligning themselves to gain importance in terms of being given authority to influence political circles, and that affiliation was -- and alignment was with the Main Staff much more in this corps than in other corps. If I understood your question correctly, and this is how I deem my answer should be given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With respect to this document, I would like to -- you to explain what they said to Mladic about who their boss was.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This is -- the way that these questions, Your Honours, are being posed is a manner that I would submit guides the witness in the formulation of his answers, and Dr. Karadzic should be cautioned to stop leading him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to the next topic, Mr. Karadzic. I think you exhausted this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to tender the document. Can it be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. I don't think we have any basis to do that now, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, yesterday on page 36 and 37 of the transcript, it was suggested to you that the policy of the SRK was to snipe at civilians in Sarajevo, and you denied that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 65 ter 23822, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, would you please look at the document and familiarise yourself with it, and tell us what you understood to be the target of the snipers in this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite clear why we decided to create conditions to secure the existence of people capable of opposing the opposing side, in this case snipers. Throughout my testimony, I tried to present the degree to which the actions of sniper forces were prevalent of the 1st Corps, and I know that the structure of those people mostly comprised Specials from the Bosna Special Brigade, and then again there was a special structure called Seve. These were people who were fatal for our forces and our composition regardless of whether we're talking about the civilian population or soldiers. I would have a whole range of indicators to present about how many drastic instances there were of sniper action directed at these people that I mentioned, whether it was soldiers or the civilian population. My escort, a policeman, soldier, who was securing the commander was hit while moving next to me. He was hit directly in the head. I'm trying to tell you here what it means to hit somebody as they're moving. I don't know why he was hit. Maybe he seemed to them to be specifically interesting person. He was very tall and thin, and perhaps they thought that they were killing me or something. I don't know. I just assumed that. There was an occasion sometimes where suddenly there would be sniper fire from one of their sniper nests, and then we had to find a solution of how to put an end to this. And there was one occasion where they had captured a key feature on the road leading to Trebevic and Pale, and I was present myself when one of the local inhabitants was driving his child to Pale to the hospital. The opposing side -- I saw this with my own eyes. The opposing side's sniper fired and shot and killed that girl. So he did not want to fire at him but at her, even though at that point that other person was closer to the sniper. So we had to introduce some sort of fight against these snipers. It was also an attempt to oppose them, but let's understand each other. This was not easy, through creating a force that would then respond to that type of fire, i.e., enemy snipers. This is a position that I know that we cultivated and that we tried to deal with that in particular. In that case, all I can say is that the existence of our snipers and their possible training and direction was just something that was done for these reasons in terms of the opposing side. There was a large number of very capable snipers on their side. Don't forget that this was Sarajevo where there were different profiles of people, and in particular I'm talking about the Specials from the Bosna Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. Did you sign this on behalf of General Galic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: One more question. This order of yours, could it have been a basis for firing at civilians in any way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course it could not have been. This is impossible. You cannot order or issue orders whereby some of those military structures of ours, regardless of which one it was, would fire at civilians. Please. There were mechanisms of internal control. If anyone knows anything about those contacts with people, then it's me, without pretensions of emphasising that is something really important, but it's true. In some contacts with fighters and while directing them how to conduct themselves, they would say to me, "General, don't you worry. We have our own controls here, because in that area there, our mothers, our sisters, fathers, are also moving around." And those who did not have their mother, father, or relatives there, then these others would warn them that when they opened fire, they should not open fire without making sure first not to direct that fire at a civilian. This is something that was taken into account, very much so, and I said a number of times that our soldiers took us to account for making so many warnings to them, but this is something that has its grounds, its logic, its causes, and it's quite normal to do this so that you don't permit people to think the way they want to think but to be disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we -- I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2902, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you stated that there were mechanisms of internal control separate from warnings you gave to them. Could you tell us in concrete terms what those internal control mechanisms were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I meant -- completely interpretation, internal, internal control. I'm formulating this in the way that I understood it and how it proceeded, and that's what it is, internal, if I may put it that way. Mutual among fighters, one's own warnings from their own reasons, security reasons so that none of their own would be -- due to some possible carelessness by those who have no relatives in Sarajevo, so that they would not be in the position to execute that action. However, that's not the only one. This is among the fighters themselves. Now, there is also a whole range of these checks and balances that are exercised by the superior officers. The selection of the location for the sniper, warning about what his task is, making sure whether they observe the target, gather the information, whether they observed sniper action. This was not difficult to notice. This could have been done by any commanding officer monitoring the situation on the ground to see where fire was coming from. If I may say this to you: The mechanical engineering faculty, one side of the building where there are no doors, no windows, there is just a wall, that area was on the Muslim side across the Miljacka River, and there were holes drilled through which snipers targeted their own targets, that they wanted to target, including the civilian population. You could monitor this from day to day, how it looked when they drilled a hole and then fired from there and then they would be exposed to fire by our sharpshooters, then he would drill a different hole in order to conceal himself and so on and so forth. And this side of the building was looking like a beehive. I don't know how the building withstood that kind of destruction to its structure. But anyway, that was the source where that was coming from. There was also the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that building, the government building. There was also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the topic you are discussing with Mr. Karadzic was whether VRS targeted civilians, and you said this order couldn't be a basis for such order, and you said there were mechanisms of internal control, but you are now talking about different things. Please concentrate on answering the question. If you think you answered the question, I give the floor to Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you receive, and in what form if you did, reports or charges or allegations about Serb soldiers firing at civilians in sniper action?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive them. These were -- let me say this was information that was coming from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you take into account information in the media, foreign, domestic, and how did you view that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The media are another topic, a separate topic. An atmosphere was being created there that was not even close to what was actually taking place on the ground. Therefore, there was an exaggeration, dramatising of the situation and a constant tendency to create an atmosphere of some wilful brutal behaviour by the fighters on our side. The media was a certain indicator, and we did attempt to think about it and to see what was true and correct of all those things, but there was so much exaggeration that it was not possible to achieve the effect of combatting this and for that media to stop launching these things. All the other information about what was happening in terms of negative actions on our part was checked and efforts were made to establish whether there was data that could indicate whether this was true or not, and then if so, orders were issued to stop with such actions regardless of the intentions of whoever was doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. By investigating allegations, did you ever establish that anybody was really guilty, and if you did, what happened to that person and who conducted this procedure further?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you just reminded me of something, and I perhaps should repeat that the extent of the activities and the tasks that the corps command had to carry out, in this case, myself at the head of that command, did not give me the opportunity to personally carry out the entire procedure. I had to do it with the assistance of the military police organs or by issuing instructions also to them or to the prosecutor's office. And I said already yesterday that by submitting criminal charges we would start the processing of those who could be accused of those guilty of violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. In that regard, what can you tell us about the degree and nature of command and control in the SRK?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I need to repeat it, as I believe I have discussed it several times. Any control of behaviour and opening fire, irrespective of its type, especially sniper fire, was such that it could prevent any such behaviour. It was sufficient. I'm not trying to say that it was absolutely excluded, though. It also had to do with potential situations which may arise during combat, and such combat developed from one day to the next or from one hour to the next. In any case, when we were not being fired at, we did not respond with fire, and that includes civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have P1201?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While waiting for the document, General, did the military police or the security and intelligence organ, as well as the system of reporting and initiating procedures, did you ever receive any information that any of those did not work properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question? It seems to me that there are two questions there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have the military police prosecution and courts at your disposal? Did you have that, and did they function properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did have it, and they functioned. Of course, there may have been weaknesses, but it was all in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last sentence of your order.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Inform me personally of the readiness to implement this task." To any soldier this sentence is crystal clear, but since you are asking me about it, it seems that an additional explanation is required in this situation. It is a basic principle whereby the commander is issuing a task, and at the same time he wants to know, first of all, whether such an order can be implemented; and if so, there are additional issues and mechanisms to be put in place which would secure the implementation of that activity as envisaged in an earlier procedure specifying when fire could be opened, under what circumstances, and which targets need to be singled out as more or less profitable or causing lesser or greater threat. Once a report comes back that the unit in question is ready to implement the task, they also need to report on its implementation. They need to confirm whether they have been able to observe the target, what was its environment, and whether there is any danger to civilians, and if there is such danger, what is its extent. The commander indeed did that and confirmed. I am not trying to say that this mechanism would remove any responsibility on my side, but I still wanted to hear from this person's mouth to what extent he was able to view the entire situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this an exception, or, rather, how did you make sure that you received information about other orders and their implementation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mutual communication and the functioning of the reporting line in terms of providing information was of the utmost importance, because in a time of war, inaccurate information can be deadly. If anyone engaged in combat according to such information could only expect to be defeated and nothing else. There should simply be no room for inaccuracy when engaging in combat, otherwise, that situation would have been fatal to us under the circumstances. Opinions or assessments had no room in that situation. I could hear their reporting, the enemy's reports on the extent of their reconnaissance and how they followed our activities. So we couldn't do -- act otherwise. We had to have a clear situation in military terms, and only then could we expect to be successful in implementing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. You said that mortars are not placed on asphalt or concrete. Can you tell us why?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it probably requires some explanation here, but it is obvious. A mortar had its base plate, it's a metal plate, which needs to be placed on soft ground, on soil, which excludes sand because it would sink. If placed on asphalt or concrete, it would bounce off once a shell is lowered into the tube and when fired. It could present a danger to the crew. After the first shell is launched, even if placed on soft ground the plate is not stable. That is why we correct fire. So after the first shot was fired, the plate needs to be readjusted again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned at that placing mortars on vehicles, which is what the 1st Corps in Sarajevo did, well, can you tell us how that affected their accuracy? How accurate were they able to be if they placed their weapons on the back of pick-up trucks, for example?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm always prepared to be corrected but I don't recall a single question or answer during the cross-examination related to mortars on vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I understood that to be related to the technical aspect whether a mortar can be installed on hard surface. That may include the truck, but I'm not sure it's really necessary, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wanted to address the issue of concrete and soil. I wanted to extend that to the issue of vehicles and trains, and how that affected accuracy as compared to other circumstances. And you understood it well, it is a technical issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I'll be brief. There's no reason not to be. The surface needs to be of such type that would sufficiently stabilise the mortar. To place a mortar on the back of a truck or train, well, it couldn't be stabilised in that way, resulting in its inaccuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, thank you. Yesterday, on pages 58 and 59, you were asked about violations of the TEZ in May 1995. You said that you were forced to defend; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 65 ter 24511.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what this document is. You see the first page. What does it discuss? We see the date, the 25th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a regular combat report. I suppose it was sent by the corps command to the Main Staff of the VRS. Of course, it was also sent to the forward command post at Trnovo. It's a regular combat report for the past 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was the main event? What was it that you had to defend from? Because you did say you had to defend yourselves.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One can see that the enemy opened fire from different kinds of weapons, that is to say, artillery weapons, mortars, and infantry weapons. We see what locations they engaged, especially the Lukavica Road, which was the road we used regularly. It seems that a Browning weapon was used in particular against our parts of Dobrinja and in Kaponiri, which is an area that had been used for anti-aircraft defence near the airport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 3. Sorry, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to the agreement about the total exclusion zone, were they allowed to engage from such weapons?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the agreement applied to them too. They shouldn't have, but they used it a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Item 8, "Conclusion," what does it tell us about enemy activities and the UN and NATO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A report needs to provide information to the Main Staff about our assessments, our forecasts of further activity. In this case, it was assessed that such activities would continue and that it would take place with the support of the units of the UN and NATO, which was to be expected in the forthcoming period. If I take our assessment into account, I can say -- or I can confirm that it did indeed developed that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was about to ask you if it indeed happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2903, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you mentioned certain wartime events in mid-June 1995. Can you tell us what it was about? You mentioned hell. Briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the problem when one needs to explain that kind of situation in only a few words, which is not an easy task. I repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, this is a question now based on Dr. Karadzic's redirect of yesterday and not arising from cross-examination. It's a clarification of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to lay a foundation for another question. General, did I undertake any measures at the time you were in the middle of that hellish situation? Did I do anything with regard to the area of the SRK? Did I institute a measure on my part as president?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I know. I think I have mentioned it during examination-in-chief. It was then that the state of war was proclaimed. It was my understanding that it was proclaimed in order to create a new situation with greater authority, without going into detail what it actually meant. It was aimed at assisting us in bearing the burden and force of attack in the situation we were in as a result of their strong offensive. What I said is what I will repeat. It was never necessary to undertake any special measures because we could feel best what our situation was. Nothing could help us other than properly managing our forces and decisively counter -- and successfully combatting their attempts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D03232?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, is the authority of civilian structures expanded in times of war and does it affect only the military or the society as a whole?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The society as a whole. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Chamber what this decision is about and why was it introduced?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't normally mean to intervene so often, but with respect, I think we're far and away outside the boundaries of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't remember the situation, but the hell issue was raised in his re-examination, as you indicated, and so that topic was -- in my opinion was related to your cross-examination. I didn't check it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, however, we're on the question of the authority of civilian structures in times of war, and this is what I think has pushed the boundaries too far, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. During the cross-examination there were many topics covered about this time period of June 1995, including dealing with the hostages, attacks on convoys. There are indictment incidents, shelling of -- use of air-bombs during this period, and I think Dr. Karadzic is entitled to show the situation that existed at that time with respect to the attacks and the -- the attacks by the Muslim forces and the offensive that was launched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll allow the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please relate to us what is stated under item 2? What was the goal? Could you please explain why I was forced to do this? What was the goal of introducing a state of war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand your question, but allow me before answering to provide you with another piece of information. It is obvious that the state of war was declared only in the zone of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. This is even more important than what you are asking me about. This implies the gravity of the situation, and it did not include the declaration of a state of war throughout Republika Srpska, and this is important for what I'm about to say. And when I try to explain the situation of our forces within the corps concerned, then this is the proper explanation. It says here the aim of declaring a state of war is to enable the full engagement of human and material potential in defence of the republic and final victory over the enemy. This is an additional assistance in support, and at that point I no longer have to beg anybody to be engaged with their capacities, with their assets, et cetera. And this implied for those structures which are not purely military, that they should obey requests coming to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2904, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You discussed, General, sir, places where you directed your retaliation against. Let me quote General Fraser on that, on page 8007. It reads here: "[In English] The Muslims fired at Lukavica with mortar, and we protested the Muslim forces for doing that because of our concern with the reaction which followed through which was -- brought a heavy artillery barrage with heavy calibre weapons back at the city."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think the first part of your quotation seems to be missing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question: "[In English] Do you recall -- you alluded to it, but do you recall the nature of the shelling of Lukavica by the Bosnian forces, the type of weaponry and the amount of death occasion -- on that occasion?" Page 8007. The answer was: "The Muslims fired at Lukavica with mortars" and so on. Next question: "And when you say 'back at the city,' was the shelling by the Bosnian Serb forces following the mortar -- the shelling of Lukavica directed at the Bosnian 1st Corps headquarter or was it directed elsewhere?" And the answer of General Fraser is: "The shelling did not come back at the Bosnian corps headquarter. It seemed to be indiscriminate across the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Why did not -- why you didn't retaliate against the corps command after they'd fired at your corps command? Where was that retaliatory fire directed at?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering if it would be of assistance to the General if this could be placed in time just a little bit, which the quote didn't do, but I think Dr. Karadzic, from reading General Fraser's evidence, is in a position to do. It just might assist the General in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, General Fraser discusses 1995, when the Muslim forces fired at Lukavica, which was your headquarters of the corps command, and he concludes -- well, he states that they protested with the Muslim forces because they expected that the SRK would retaliate. And then he states that you do not retaliate at the 1st Corps command headquarters but elsewhere in the city. Could you please tell us which points was your fire directed at? I'm tying this to your answer to the Prosecution that you did not fire at their command posts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did understand everything. My explanation stands, and it is this: It is true we did not fire at command posts. Let's take into consideration that those command posts were within the city. Let me remind you that their command corps, the 1st Command Corps was in the centre of the city in Danila Ozme [phoen] Street, that the 12th Brigade was close to Skenderija, very close to tenement buildings, et cetera. From my point of view, it would mean nothing to me if we were to threaten their command post. They had ample structures that they could perform their command duties with if -- even if their headquarters were destroyed. What we wanted to do is to find those who fired at us, and that was the target for us, for our firing. I will have to try to explain to the Chamber that this term "retaliation" is not proper. This is not appropriate because it sounds too drastic to me, but in essence, it is a legitimate term as a term, as a notion. But this was not retaliation. We were trying to find the targets that we could preclude their firing at Lukavica. Fire in this case, with all due respect to what General Fraser stated, what I do know is that I knew the situation much better than whoever appeared here testifying in this or that case, and I know that their fire was targeted not just at our command post but at civilians and the buildings surrounding the command corps -- command post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's clarify the transcript. Page 30, line 13. General, did you say, "It is true that we did fire at command posts"? I understood you told us that: "It is true that we did not fire at command posts."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that we did not fire at command posts, absolutely. Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to correct the transcript, the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Being mindful of the time, I would need another 15 minutes, Your Excellencies, by your leave, since we've lost quite a lot of time, and with due respect, you did take -- did ask some questions. Should we stop now or should we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll have break for half an hour and resume at 3 past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, allow me to introduce another member of our team, Eva Suboticki [phoen], from Belgrade, who is together with us in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, on page 81 of yesterday's transcript, it seems to me, it was suggested to you that retaliation was directed against the centre of Hrasnica and that it took place substantially afterwards. Do you know -- well, the document of the UN states when that retaliation took place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we take a look at D2817, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you did not say it was retaliation but silencing those assets, although you avoided the term "retaliation," although it is a legitimate action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton. Without having to turn to you. It's evidently a very leading question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The General stated that he was not talking about retaliation. He was talking about seeking the targets to silence them, and this is what he said. It was suggested to him that that retaliation took place substantially afterwards, as stated on page 81, and that it was retaliation rather than trying to silence those assets. Could we please refer to the relevant page. Next page, please. The Sarajevo Sector. I'm going to read out loud. [In English] "The situation is assessed to remain stable. The level of firing incidents will likely continue to rise. The rocket which impacted in Hrasnica was most likely retaliation for the mortar round fired from Hrasnica some minutes before."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, did this response or retaliation took place in a timely manner or was it postponed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in a timely manner, and this is corroborated by this document. I can see the content in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, General Fraser testified here that mortars could not destroy buildings in Sarajevo because such buildings were built of concrete. Are the Turkish part and the Austro-Hungarian part of Sarajevo, are they built of concrete?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic provide a citation, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That would be page 009 and 00 -- 8010. Can you remember that question about whether concrete was used to build the Turkish and the Austro-Hungarian parts of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do recall the question. It is quite clear that in Turkish times, during the Ottoman times, they could build using stone, not steel or concrete. As far as the Austro-Hungarian part of the town is concerned, they could have used concrete partly. Buildings, however, built of concrete -- well, buildings which are firm and stable do not have to be built of concrete. They could have used other materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have only mortars at your disposal or did you have at your disposal other pieces of artillery that could have been used to destroy buildings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We did not use other assets that could destroy whole buildings. It goes for assets that are considered such as missiles, rockets, they're not intended to destroy facilities, buildings, fortifications of that kind. These are first and foremost anti-armour assets which have -- which generate high temperatures on impact to melt steel. None of such assets, such rockets or missiles, could have such an impact on a building. These are primarily anti-armour assets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many buildings in Sarajevo were destroyed? We're not talking about being pockmarked or damaged.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any buildings being torn down or destroyed. What I know about Sarajevo and what I could see for myself, Sarajevo was not destroyed. There were no destroyed buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many mosques did you tear down using artillery? How many schools, kindergartens were destroyed by artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this question. It means a lot to me to be able to talk about that. The Muslim forces were mindful of this. Within Sarajevo, there are many mosques at different locations and those mosques and their turrets, these are prominent positions and features. For some of their reasons they did not want to use such areas, such localities for opening fire at us, which could not be said of other prominent positions within the city, and therefore they did not create the conditions where we had to return fire at those positions if such fire was intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, did you have observers where you deployed your artillery?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you receive warnings from them to the effect that you opened fire without observing the procedure, without having received information from them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The situation was this: They could see for themselves. They could observe what was going on close to our artillery assets to warn of movements and activities and provide facts of the situation on the ground. So no such situations occurred apart from regular reporting back on developments in a certain area. Well, sometimes the situations were blown up out of proportion in certain cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure about "naduvavanje" [phoen], the way it was interpreted. What did you want to say by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exaggerating, reporting that something was happening even though it was evident that that data -- or actually such an action could not have even taken place. For example, when one of the observers, I've forgotten his name now, either from the UNPROFOR sector and he happened to be in that particular zone, reported, and it even seems to me that he testified that from Spicasta Stijena, which was created as a myth, as a concept, a "stena" [phoen], as being something in particular, that he saw an air-bomb being launched from that place. First of all, how could that combat asset, the way it was built and in view of its structure, even get to such a -- as it was described, I would say, this Spicasta Stijena and that it was talked about as if it was as great as a goddess. So there was talk about something that could not be accepted, and I don't know who accepted that, and I don't know how the Prosecution can use such an assertion about a spot and about how impossible it was to launch an air-bomb from an elevation like that. I mean, a vehicle would need to approach that point and one would need to take care that the vehicle would not be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how would you assess the precision of reporting by the military observers according to what reached you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two assessments. There were, proper, correct, and precise reports, assessment of the situation in the field, what was observed, and also, believe me, there was reporting that was actually meant to satisfy the opposing side without proving that in any particular way. Now I'm talking about my impression and about some data that I had at my disposal, but these times are over now so I can no longer locate them in terms of their precise formulation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at D2823 now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before doing so, I wonder whether the General has answered your question at all, i.e., the question as to: "How many mosques did you tear down using artillery? How many schools, kindergartens were destroyed by artillery fire?" Did you answer the question? Whatever the reason it might have been. How many mosques, schools, kindergartens were destroyed by artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we did not destroy any of the schools or mosques. This is what I know, what I am aware of, particularly when we're talking about kindergartens and schools. However much it's clear that those schools were used for wrong purposes, it's also clear that they were not targeted, and they were not destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So how many mosques that were used for the military purpose were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked about mosques located directly in the city, thus in that area of Bascarsija, in the centre area of Sarajevo. That was that area that was covered with them, and no fire was opened at those mosques. They were not destroyed, nor did my opponents fire from those positions and that is why it was protected and they were not to be fired at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at D2823 for a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, are you able to tell us how, on the basis of this document, it can be concluded that you were at the forward command post? Do you remember this document? It was admitted.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is quite clear and unequivocal, and it's not difficult to explain. I have already said a sufficient number of times that we had the situation when a part of the command, either the commander or somebody from the command, had to be even at two forward command posts besides the main one in Lukavica. When I was at the forward command post, regardless of whether it was at Nisici or the one in Trnovo, which was a settlement, when a report is being processed, thus the operations centre and the command would compile all the relevant data at the command post from the units located in the outside sectors as well as in the city itself, and when they process that they are obliged to submit that to me at the forward command post so that I would know what the status was in the other parts of the front and not only at the section of the front where I happened to be that point of time. That was the established procedure and data that would explain why this would be sent, because all the reports were not sent to the forward command post when somebody was not there at the forward command post, when the commander was not there. But I was quite frequently at the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 82 of yesterday's transcript, it was suggested to you that there were no mines being produced at the Aleksa Santic school but only the casings were cast there. Does shell -- casting of the casing, is that a part of shell manufacture?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any part of the -- or any stage of production process of a lethal device would mean that wherever that production took place, that would be a potential military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was suggested to you, and Brko Zecevic changed this, that some asset which exploded in Dositejeva Street was actually a modified air-bomb launched from Vogosca. What is the range and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think there's been some misstatements of things that I'm alleged to have suggested. First of all, the question with respect to the Aleksa Santic school or the evidence with respect to the Aleksa Santic school didn't even use the word "casting." The evidence that was put to the witness was, at page 33162, to the effect that a previous Defence witness said specifically there was no production going on in the school and the only thing going on was melting in the gym. Nothing to do with the word "casting." Now, with respect to Dositejeva Street, although I struggled to find the citation at speed, the reference -- there was, to my recollection, absolutely no suggestion as to the origin of fire of where the bomb might have fallen on Dositejeva Street. The question was simply related to the witness's statement and his examination-in-chief to the effect that if an air-bomb had fallen, the damage would have been much greater. So I think these are a couple of misstatements now that Dr. Karadzic is putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, can you melt steel or iron in one place and then take it for casting at a different place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not an expert in this, but based on what I know and what seems logical to me, any kind of action that has to do with casting steel or any other materials has its own procedure, and I'm not able to interpret it in any other way other than an action that has to do with the preparation of an asset for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 69 of the transcript, you were asked about Dositejeva. I'm asking you now: What is the range of those rockets that would bear an air-bomb and would one that was fired from Vogosca be observed by observers or by just regular citizens? Would it be visible?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if -- if we're going down the road of technical analysis, I -- which was not raised in cross-examination, I may, I feel I should indicate now, be looking for an opportunity to re-cross on this technical evidence, and that would not be a matter I would be able to do immediately but would need just a little bit of time to prepare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree. Could you move on to other things, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will move to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, would it happen that something would be ascribed to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps that you did not do, practically something that was done by someone else? That the 1st Corps did to itself.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have the opportunity ever to state my knowledge and activity that I expressed in order to get to something that represents data as to what happened when, and if I am permitted and if I'm given the opportunity to say so now, that would be the following: It was established that on the 4th of February, 1994, it was the 4th or the 5th of February, 1994, a mine dropped on the market, the Markale Market. This was something that constituted a horrendous --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a second. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Another area, Your Honours, that was squarely not within the bounds of cross-examination, and if we're going to come to detailed evidence with regard to this incident, I would be requesting Your Honours' leave to re-cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, just -- we won't go there. I'm not sure how this arose from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, the Prosecution suggested that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps fired heavy weaponry at Sarajevo on the basis of statements by many that explosions were heard and that damage to buildings was visible. I am asking my question on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were those people able to see something that the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, this has nothing to do with his cross-examination. If you have nothing else, please conclude your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, sir, did you and I ever discuss the question of, as they're called here, modified air-bombs and their use?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is no conversation on that topic between you and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At any meetings that were attended both by you and I, was there any mention of air-bombs, about their precision or lack of precision or generally about their use? And it's not whether the two of us discussed it but whether this topic was ever mentioned in any meeting attended by other people.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was never any mention, discussion, in-depth consideration of the use of air-bombs and their effects. I do not recall now any specific meeting where that came up as a topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was I present at any of such meetings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR MILOSEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is why I'm saying that I do not recall anything like that ever taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, sir, are you able to tell us briefly --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- I am asking to re-cross on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Excellencies. I am not going to go on any more so as not to put the Prosecution in a position to seek more. In any case, after 17 years to seek more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to show a document of Croatian origin, but you would not allow me to show who creates and how evidence is planted as to who committed what.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no idea what Dr. Karadzic is talking about, but if I am able to -- if this concludes his testimony and I can re-cross, if I could just have a couple of moments, I need to find a citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he concluded his re-examination. Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. With the remark that I had some documents to show as well, but the conclusion of the Trial Chamber is that this does not arise from the cross-examination, so I am leaving that out. I will not show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Before any re-cross-examination, I think the Prosecution should ask for the permission of the Chamber and be specific as to what they want to ask about and why they couldn't ask it during their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think the issue regarding the meeting or conversation between Mr. Karadzic and the General on the topics related to air-bombs was discussed in the cross-examination, and since this was raised in his re-examination, it's fair enough for Ms. Edgerton to have one more go if necessary. I think the issue is related to -- to that topic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. The issue is related to Dr. Karadzic's notice or awareness of the use of modified air-bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I still struggle to find the P number in yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: General, just in relation to the point that you've discussed with Dr. Karadzic where you've given evidence to the effect that during meetings and conversations with him at which you might have been present, you never heard the use of modified air-bombs discussed, I'd like to know are you -- are you disputing -- does that mean that you're disputing that Dr. Karadzic received reports about the use of these assets?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think that's a fair question now. That's going beyond the question. If -- if she has information that at meetings at which he was present or they attended together the topic was discussed, then she can ask it, but now she's the one trying to expand it beyond the scope and that would not be fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I will if I can just have your indulgence for a couple of moments to find the citation to the document I'm looking for, I'll be in a better position to deal with it. Please, your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I may assist, Your Excellency. I asked whether I was present anywhere when the imprecision of the air-bombs was discussed. Was my attention drawn to the fact that the weapon was imprecise. Precision was discussed in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that Mr. Robinson is distinguishing, drawing a line between information at meetings and actual notice, and I think given the time it might take to pursue and argue that issue, it's in the interests of everyone to leave it at that and rely on the evidence that was previously adduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Appreciate it, Ms. Edgerton. Thank you. Then unless my colleagues have questions for you -- yes. Yes. Then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Milosevic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it. Now you're free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I also thank you, Mr. Bourgon, and the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I'll be giving my chair over to Mr. Vanderpuye and take my leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next witness to be brought in, I will give an oral ruling.
