utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll start this clip at 8.29, and this is from a radio you gave in 2010, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "Welcome back to issues, et cetera --"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We'll start this at 8.29 so that we can move along quicker.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: "ST: ... Their ways and their habits. "J: With only about 30 seconds, what specifically can be done in France and other Western European countries to stem the tide of Islamic extremism? About 30 seconds, Srdja. "ST: To lower the number of the Muslim diaspora in those countries. "J: How is that done? "ST: By a variety of legal means, above all by the definition of Islamism as a political and not religious affiliation which would be the grounds not only for the denial of citizenship but also for removal. "J: So you're talking about not only new immigration policies based upon Islamist adherence but also perhaps even -- what? "ST: Deportation. Deportation. Let's be quite frank about it. If you support an ideology that is inherently seditious and detrimental to the objectives, goals, and dynamics of a democratic state, then you do not belong. And for any Muslim to claim that, on the one hand, they can be supportive of the mandated violence against infidels and institutionalised discrimination against them that is contained in the Koran and at the same time they can swear an oath of allegiance when they become new citizens, on the other hand, is simply incongruous. To a truly devout Muslim, the Koran and Shari'ah is the only legitimate source of loyalty. Of course they can swear allegiance to the United States because they practice taqiyah -- "J: About ten seconds here. "ST: But let me sum it up by saying that the fewer Muslims there are in a non-Muslim society, the more harmonious and the less likely to be hit by terrorist violence it is. "J: Dr. Srdja Trifkovic is director of the --"

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall that interview, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's you speaking?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this exhibit. I think I made a mistake with respect to the -- the 65 ter number is 24539A, because it's a clip of the larger recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I couldn't found -- find it with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, since it was played in full, I don't see the purpose of tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It was played from 8.29 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's reflected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- through 10.19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There's no need to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I correct if I say that we would need to hear the question regarding this interview and not just hear that he gave an interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What we heard has been reflected in the transcript. So you'd like to admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. But I didn't understand that. It was not being admitted. However, I didn't hear the question. What is the Prosecutor's question to the witness about the interview, other than just the fact that he gave the interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you heard that. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you have about seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You say in your statement that you went down to see Dr. Karadzic in Pale, you left Belgrade -- well, you went there on the 13th of July, 1995, and met with him from about 1700 hours to 1840; correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact you left Belgrade on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With Mrs. Ristic and Mr. Premovic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You arrived in Pale on the 12th and you had some informal talks with Jovan Zametica and Zdravko Miocic; right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I asked you about that conversation with Mr. Miocic on the 12th of July during your testimony in the Popovic case; right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you didn't recall precisely what that conversation concerned; right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I asked you what specifically Dr. Karadzic said to you during the time that you met with him on 13 July concerning what was happening in relation to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you are unable to recall what he said because you said you lost your notes and your laptop failed you at some point?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. But I did have broad recollection about his optimistic demeanour and his insistence that civilians be treated properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. You said that you didn't recall exactly what he said because of your lack of precise notes and that you could only provide the best of your recollection at that time after 13 years; right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I asked you again about the details of what was discussed during the meeting with Dr. Karadzic on the 13th, and you gave this answer: "I have to confine myself to overall impressions because I don't have the minutes, and after all this time, the memories tend to acquire the character of overall impressions rather than specific snippets or quotes."

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, that's at transcript reference -- Popovic transcript reference 2576 -- 25276, sorry, line 17, through 25277, line 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Again I asked you about the extent of your recollection of that meeting, and you gave it this way. You said specifically this: "... I recall -- what I recall of that meeting is, first of all, a very long discourse on the end game which he," Dr. Karadzic, "confidently expected to follow that would be favourable to the Serbian point of view; and secondly, the agreement with my insistence that it is both substantially and in terms of media relations extremely important to avoid any incidents in the treatment of civilian -- of the civilian population that would be reminiscent of the early stages of the war." Yes?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's at transcript reference 25280, lines 8 through 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In your statement, you've added a couple of snippets, as you call it. One is that you expected General Mladic to call.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I have not read my 2008 testimony before coming here today, but I believe that I have mentioned it, that episode with a phone call or, rather, the call that was not to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recall my asking you during the course of your Popovic testimony that -- whether or not during your meeting with Dr. Karadzic he was in contact with anybody else, including any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't specifically remember, but I would appreciate being reminded.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, that's at transcript page reference 25272, lines 5 through 6. I asked you that question, and in your response you never mentioned that Dr. Karadzic spoke to any soldier, and you never mentioned that Dr. Karadzic ever expected any call from General Mladic. And that's throughout your testimony.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the what?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Throughout your testimony, you do not mention at all that Dr. Karadzic or you expected any phone call from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I remember positively mentioning this in this court, is it possible that it may have been stated in the testimony in the Stakic case --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I don't believe so --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: -- because --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- but in any event, it wasn't stated in the Popovic case, which is what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mentioned in your statement at paragraph 30 that one of the reasons why you picked up the phone was to get a quote from General Mladic about the circumstances in which he was involved; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And one of the reasons you went down to Pale to begin with was in order to get certain information for the purposes of your media interviews.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So when you went there - and that's what you said in the Popovic case - did it somehow slip your mind that you wanted to speak to General Mladic, among other people that you wanted to speak to, which was the reason for your going to Pale to begin with?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The reason I failed to mention that phone call is that it was unimportant, because there was no Mladic at the other end of the line. It simply didn't seem significant, because there was nothing of substance told by whoever replied and told Dr. Karadzic that Mladic is unavailable. But, yes, it was my purpose to obtain as many statements from as many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you know that Ms. Ristic and Mr. Premovic testified in this case, do you not?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did you learn that? Did the Defence tell you that?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I actually found it on Google and there were some articles in the former Yugoslav press.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so you know --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I also had an e-mail from Mr. Premovic saying that he had just come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just come back from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you talk to Mr. Premovic or Ms. Ristic about what they said, what they testified in this case, sir?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke to Mr. Premovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mr. Premovic told you that he said during this case or his evidence in this case is that Dr. Karadzic spoke to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that he was under the impression Dr. Karadzic spoke to General Mladic but that in retrospect he cannot be certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And Ms. Ristic --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- did you speak to her?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Having gone to Pale from Belgrade to find out what the position of the RS leadership was going to be in respect of the events concerning Srebrenica, did it somehow slip your mind that Momcilo Krajisnik was in that office that day during the period of time that you were meeting with Dr. Karadzic too?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: On previous occasions I found Mr. Krajisnik's assessments and the value of his analysis less than impressive. I actually didn't regard it as particularly useful to try and get a statement from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But you remember him being there. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't specifically remember him being there, but I wouldn't be surprised. I wasn't specifically seeking him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't mention him during the course of your Popovic testimony with regard to the events on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You did not mention him during your Popovic testimony with regard to the events that occurred on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Why should I mention him?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Because you were asked who else was present during the course of the time that you were meeting with the president.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: But no words were exchanged, no statement was required. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A while ago your time's up, so I would like you to ask your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, you referred to this Tribunal in a number of articles as doing the bidding as a political tool for its political bosses and paymasters as a pseudo-legal imposter, as a fraud, as an Orwellian institution whose unanimous decisions are as drearily predictable as those in Moscow in 1936, as an institution that exists solely to proclaim the Serbs collectively as the guilty party for everything that has happened in the Balkans to retroactively justify Western policy. You've said that the Prosecutors at The Hague will try to pit Karadzic against Mladic, and you have said of both Karadzic and Mladic that they will be duly convicted of genocide and crimes against humanity, that they will not come out of gaol alive and the verdict is already written. Is it your expectation here today that knowing all of that and your background and views about Islam and Muslims, is it your expectation that the Chamber should rely on your evidence as credible and reliable in respect of the incidents -- or in respect of what you've stated in your statement concerning the events --

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- of 13 July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No qualms about it?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions. I do want to tender the parts of the Popovic transcript that I have indicated. I can do that at a later time if that would be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will be objecting to that, Mr. President, so maybe he can do that in writing. But if there's been some portion of the Popovic case that is inconsistent with his testimony, then it could possibly be admitted, but he used the technique of reading out swathes of the Popovic evidence and having the witness confirm it and there would be no value to admitting the transcript of that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to forestall any unnecessary discussion by way of what I understand to be the practice of the Court, if the witness confirmed it, then I think the Court has taken the position in the past it's not necessary; if there was no such confirmation, then the excerpts are admissible and I don't think Mr. Robinson would indeed object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit those pages referred to in his cross-examination. If you could liaise with the Registrar as well as the Defence in identifying the -- those page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will do, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That concludes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. -- just a second. Yes. We will give the number for that Popovic transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Exhibit P6102.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellency, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Trifkovic, today, on page 93, it was suggested to you that I expected a call from Mladic. And on page 95 what was read out to you was that it was said that Mladic is unavailable. Are you able to tell us who called and who expected?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad you asked this, because it was only subsequent to my testimony in 2008 that this failed attempt at establishing contact seems to have acquired undue significance. My impression is that you were trying to contact Mladic and that you were repeatedly inquiring with the secretary what's up with the lines and that she once or twice replied the lines were down. And you asked her to keep trying, and then she came back at one point saying that he's on the other line and it turned out that it wasn't him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 89, there was a quote that in your lecture, I think, you made a difference between Islam and Islamism. Are you able to tell us what the difference is?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It is the key difference and it is also the one distinction that I made in my radio interview. Islamism is a political ideology that seeks to introduce Shari'a as the basis of the legal and political system, and that seeks to uphold the tenets of Islamic scriptures and historical practice as the basis of socio-political and legal order. In that sense, Islamism is a totalitarian ideology on par with Bolshevism or National Socialism. And being engaged in Islamist activities, it is my firm belief is not only incompatible with the values of a democratic society but also should be the grounds for the exclusion of the person just as to this day if you answer positively to the question about the membership in certain fringe political parties, you will be denied a US visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the work of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Islamic writers? Do you know any of their work?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously Alija Izetbegovic's Islamic Declaration comes to mind, but I have been acquainted only with certain interesting quotes rather than read the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to what you know about the text, would that be an Islamic or an Islamist text?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It is firmly in the latter category because, and I'm quoting from memory but I believe accurately, Izetbegovic stated that there can be no peace and long-term co-existence between Islam and other forms of political organisation, and goes on to advocate a single umma, the community of the faithful, spreading from Morocco in the west to Indonesia in the east. And he goes further to attack the legacy of Mustafa Kemel -- Kemel Ataturk, and to say that in the Ottoman period as a Halifat, Turkey was a great and glorious power, and as a secular republic under Ataturk's successors, it has become a second-rate nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is then your position towards Islam in comparison to Islamism?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the key point, that Islam as a domain of the private set of beliefs and practices of individuals can be accommodated into a democratic society, but Islamism with its demand for constant activism in the escalation of special privileges for the members of the Islamic Community in fact will never be satisfied with any given outcome. And historical evidence clearly points that having achieved one level of acceptance and exemptions and special privileges, an Islamist will immediately proceed to the next one. Because just as a convinced Communist will not rest until the world has been subjected to the proletarian revolution, likewise an Islamist cannot accept the division of the world into Dar al-Islam, the world of faith, and Dar al-Harb, the world of war, as a permanent given. He sees his task to expend the sphere of Dar al-Islam at the expense of Dar al-Harb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 87 of today's transcript, you were denied the opportunity to say what you meant under psychosis. Can you briefly just tell us what you meant under psychosis?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, exactly this Manakian [phoen] view of world as us and them. Dar al-Islam, the world of faith, Dar al-Harb, the world of war or disbelief, and that this constant tension which it creates along the edges where the Islamic world meets non-Islam, it creates conflicts that are manifested from Mindanao in the Philippines and East Timor through the Indian subcontinent, most notably Kashmir, into the Caucasus, North Africa and the Balkans, not to mention the perennial Arab-Israeli conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we will leave that topic now. I wanted to ask you to answer a few questions. Did you know by what means was the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina resolved?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was fairly familiar with the political events that preceded the outbreak of the war, and I was somewhat acquainted with the mix of military operations and diplomacy that characterized the war years. I was interested to see that there were short bursts of intense military activity followed by prolonged periods of truce during which diplomatic solutions were being attempted, and it is my view that the ultimate outcome of the Bosnia war at Dayton in the fall of 1995 is the kind of solution that could have been obtained at the very beginning with the Cutileiro Plan, which was unfortunately torpedoed by then US ambassador in Belgrade Warren Zimmermann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I was curious to see where the question and answer were going, but I can see that they go well beyond any cross-examination of this witness on any factual issues concerning the war, so I would object to any further inquiry along this line.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I need to respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor confronted the witness with military document, whereas the witness was familiar with the political position. So I have the right to clarify what the witness meant and what he knew and what is consistent as he said on page 73. He said something was not consistent. So I wanted to ask him what was relevant in that crisis. I don't want to go on to avoid leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't see it's related to -- or it arose from the line of cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Robinson, would you like to assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. Maybe I should just indicate that this entire re-direct examination is contrary to my advice to Dr. Karadzic, but I don't have anything to help you with or him at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Mr. Karadzic, move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, this was the introduction for the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of what the political position was? You said there that we said that we were not going to defeat them. Are you familiar with the position of the Serbian side regarding the military and political outcome?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's the same objection, Mr. President. Dr. Trifkovic was confronted with certain information which was responsive to what he states at paragraph 20 of his statement which was admitted into evidence in this case. The mere fact that he's confronted with documents that contradict what he says in his statement does not open up grounds for redirect on that same topic. The mere challenging of information does not create grounds for redirect examination in our jurisprudence, so I object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot -- I cannot lay the basis of a document that I want to show if that is so. The witness was shown two directives. I would like you to look at that. These were military documents. I wanted to show political documents and ask the witness what was consistent with his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone should be switched off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we just lost some lines of question. If it is related to your consistency, that may be put, but I'm not sure whether question was necessarily related to that issue. Could you let us know the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Excellencies. Directive number 4 was quoted implying that I signed it, and Directive 7 was shown to the witness. These were military documents. What I want to is to ask the witness what his knowledge is about political positions, about the political aspect, how our political actions relate to those directives. And it all has to do with my having possibly misinformed him about our political positions, and I wanted to show documents to see whether his information stemmed from these documents, the political documents, or from the military documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So political positions in the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of the political leadership of Republika Srpska, because this was something that was disputed. There was an implication that the witness was deceived, that he was deceived by wrong information, that he was misled. This was on page 70 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to respond, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As I indicated previously, the documents that were shown to the witness were directly responsive to paragraph 20 of the statement that was led by Dr. Karadzic, in particular where it states that one of Dr. Karadzic's views, which I think I read to the witness during the course of the question that Dr. Karadzic is concerned about, one of Dr. Karadzic's views was that the Serb side did not want to defeat the Muslims militarily but that each constituent nation should become master of its own fate. That's in paragraph 20 of the statement. And also, as reiterated in an interview that the witness gave previously, those documents were put to the witness in response to those specific assertions. If Dr. Karadzic sought to adduce from this witness either a distinction between the political and the military views or approaches, he could have done that certainly on direct examination. This is his evidence that we're responding to. There was nothing preventing Dr. Karadzic from leading that evidence in relation to clarifying what is meant in paragraph 20 of the 92 ter statement. So I don't think that merely responding to those -- to that assertion, particularly as respects defeating the Muslims militarily by showing the doctor military documents opens up an avenue for him to then put political documents to the -- to the doctor in response on redirect. I just don't think there's sufficient grounds that have been created during the course of the cross-examination for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But by showing the military document, you challenged the credibility of witness's statement about Mr. Karadzic's position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the military defeat of the Muslim -- of the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Robinson, do you have any observation?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As much as I hate to see Dr. Karadzic spending his time on this, I think that this is well within the cross-examination and you've already hit the nail on the head. They can't limit it such -- that way. They're trying to show that this witness was misinformed or mistaken as the views of Dr. Karadzic and he can -- it should be entitled to show those views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation. We'll allow the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly show the witness D104. D104.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, it was suggested to you that Directive 4 from November 1992 served as a directive for the expulsion of Muslims. Can you please look to see what the document refers to. The document is dated March 1993, regarding the Geneva Conventions and humanitarian aid, and is this consistent with your information as to the positions of the political leadership?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document would broadly correspond to the kind of information that you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please not overlap with the English translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Trifkovic, could you put a pause. The interpreters are not able to hear you because of the overlapping. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Article 3 of this document would broadly fit in with the views and positions that you and the late Professor Koljevic expressed concerning the application of the rules of war and the treatment of civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at D43 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document from April 1993, and it states here in paragraph 1 -- actually, cease all operations against Srebrenica; two, stop the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska; three, facilitate the passage of humanitarian activities. Second paragraph of item 5: Provide protection for all civilians. And 7: Carry the order out immediately and fully inform me thereof. Is this consistent with your understanding of the political position of the leadership of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is broadly consistent with what I understood to be the political position of the Republika Srpska leadership.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at P2276 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a report by the Main Staff of the 7th of July issued after Directive 7, which was shown to you as the source of all the difficulties and as evidence that you did not have correct information as to the positions of the Republika Srpska leadership. Could you please look at this last paragraph: In accordance with the order of the president of the republic to offer maximum protection and safety to all UNPROFOR around Srebrenica and the civilian Muslim population, you must order subordinate units to refrain from, and so on and so forth. You don't have to hear me read it. You can see it in the English.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this and in what way is this consistent with the information you had about the position of the Serbian leadership?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The final paragraph is consistent with the views you expressed on the need for the protection of civilians during the meeting on the afternoon of July 13th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we briefly look at P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you take a look at the second paragraph of this document. "The president of the republic is satisfied with the result of combat operations around Srebrenica and has agreed with the continuation of operations for the take-over of Srebrenica, disarming Muslim terrorists, disarming of Muslim terrorist gangs, and complete demilitarisation of the Srebrenica enclave." Is it consistent with what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when I was leaving for Pale, I was not aware that Srebrenica had in fact fallen, and it was only when we were - Mr. Premovic, Mrs. Ristic and I - on the road, that from the soldiers manning the roadblocks between Zvornik and Bratunac we learnt that Srebrenica had in fact fallen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question was whether it was consistent with what you knew in 1994 of Bosnian Serb leadership as you indicated in paragraph 20.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was always aware of dissatisfaction with the failure of the UN to demilitarise the so-called protected zones, even though I cannot pinpoint dates or statements, but I was broadly aware of the frustration with -- which was reiterated on my arrival in July of 1995, the frustration with the fact that demilitarised -- demilitarisation had not been carried out in the protected zones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we briefly just show two documents. P2994. This is the one. Document is dated the 11th of July. Could you please look at paragraph 3, where the establishment of civilian rule is being discussed and that of the police. And if you've looked at that, can we then look at paragraph 4. Can we look at paragraph 4 in the Serbian version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 11th, Dr. Trifkovic. Is this different from what you heard, learned from us on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, it's consistent even though I must say that in my meetings with Dr. Koljevic and you, there was no mention of military prisoners. There was no mention of POWs as such. I only recall the insistence on the need to protect and supply the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But would you agree this is confidential? It should say "strictly confidential," but it wasn't translated as strictly confidential; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It says "confidential," yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at D2055 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at item 4. This document appoints a civilian commissioner who is supposed to care for civilians and property. You don't have to read it out loud. You can read it for yourself.

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How does this fit into your knowledge about the political positions and humanitarian positions of the Republika Srpska leadership?

utterances.speaker: SRDJAN TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: My answer is broadly the same as the previous one. While I was not aware of any specific directives concerning the treatment of prisoners of war, I do recall your insistence on the correct treatment of the civilians and Professor Koljevic's stated intention to go to Srebrenica to reassure the civilians and to help arrange the smooth transition to regular authority of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Dr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless my colleagues have questions for you, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are free to go, but we'll rise all together. I thank the staff for their indulgence as well. We continue tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I ask something. Should my limitation of meeting Mr. -- General Milosevic be removed, now no reason for restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it's for the Chamber to intervene -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's pursuant to your order, Mr. President, so I think if you don't intervene -- your order is that they be segregated. But since the spirit of the order is to avoid them having contact before his testimony, we would ask that you allow or direct that he be allowed at least to meet with General Milosevic to thank him and say good-bye to him before he leaves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I don't have a useful one. I mean, my reflexive reaction is one of caution and not to lift the restriction. I just don't know if that's fair under the circumstances. We can get back to you within about 10 to 15 minutes, Mr. President. I know you don't necessarily have to make the order from the Bench and we can upon just a moment's reflection give you some feedback that may be more meaningful than just a seat-of-the-pants reaction. Obviously I don't anticipate he be recalled for any reason. I can't think offhand of how such contact would contaminate other aspects of the case, but I think it's worth thinking about for at least a few minutes before we respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the Chamber sees no difficulty with it, I will leave it to the Registrar and the commander of the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.56 p.m.,
